title: Styles and Your Learning Path
lessons/basics-u3-l1/title: Trading Styles: Scalp, Day, Swing, Position
lessons/basics-u3-l1/steps/0/body: Your trading style is mostly defined by **how long you hold a position**: **scalping** lasts seconds to minutes, **day trading** stays within the same day, **swing trading** runs days to weeks, and **position trading** lasts weeks to months.
lessons/basics-u3-l1/steps/0/tip: The timeframes next to each style are just the most common ones, not rules.
lessons/basics-u3-l1/steps/1/pairs/1/mea: Opened and closed the same day
lessons/basics-u3-l1/steps/1/pairs/2/mea: A few days to a few weeks
lessons/basics-u3-l1/steps/1/pairs/3/mea: A few weeks to a few months
lessons/basics-u3-l1/steps/2/body: A **scalper** takes lots of trades with small targets, so the **spread and commission** eat a big share of the profit, and they have to watch the charts constantly. A **swing trader** spends less time, but uses wider stops and has to live with **overnight and weekend risk** (gaps and swaps).
lessons/basics-u3-l1/steps/3/statement: For a scalper, costs like the spread and commission matter less than for a swing trader.
lessons/basics-u3-l1/steps/3/explanation: It's the opposite. A scalper takes far more trades with targets of just a few pips, so the cost of each trade eats a bigger percentage of the profit.
lessons/basics-u3-l1/steps/4/prompt: Which feature is unique to day trading?
lessons/basics-u3-l1/steps/4/options/0: Positions are closed before the day ends
lessons/basics-u3-l1/steps/4/options/1: Positions usually stay open for months
lessons/basics-u3-l1/steps/4/options/2: Analysis is done only on the weekly chart
lessons/basics-u3-l1/steps/4/options/3: Trades are always opened without a stop loss
lessons/basics-u3-l1/steps/4/explanation: A day trader doesn't hold positions overnight, so they pay no overnight swap and are safe from overnight gaps.
lessons/basics-u3-l1/steps/5/prompt: This is a 4-hour chart. The trade opened on the first candle and hit take profit on the last one. Which style is it closest to?
lessons/basics-u3-l1/steps/5/explanation: 12 candles × 4 hours = 48 hours, so the trade stayed open about 2 days and held overnight. That's a swing trade: not a few-minute scalp, not a same-day day trade, not a months-long position.
lessons/basics-u3-l1/steps/6/title: Match your style to your life
lessons/basics-u3-l1/steps/6/body: The best style is the one that fits your **free time**, **personality** and **capital**. Someone with a full-time job is usually more comfortable swing trading, while someone who enjoys quick decisions might go for day trading. **No style is naturally more profitable.**
lessons/basics-u3-l1/steps/6/tip: Many coaches suggest higher timeframes for beginners: you get more time to think.
lessons/basics-u3-l1/steps/7/prompt: Sara works an office job and only has about an hour in the evenings. Which style makes the most sense for her?
lessons/basics-u3-l1/steps/7/explanation: Swing trading works on the 4-hour and daily charts, and checking once a day is enough. Scalping and day trading need you there constantly during the day.
lessons/basics-u3-l1/steps/8/prompt: Order the styles from the shortest holding time to the longest.
lessons/basics-u3-l1/steps/8/explanation: Scalping lasts minutes, day trading hours (within one day), swing trading days to weeks, and position trading weeks to months.
lessons/basics-u3-l2/steps/0/body: In forex you trade through a **broker**. You usually trade a contract on the **price change** and never receive the currency itself. A **crypto exchange** matches buyers with sellers, and you can buy the actual coin and move it to your wallet.
lessons/basics-u3-l2/steps/1/prompt: You want to buy real Bitcoin and move it to your personal wallet. Where can you do that?
lessons/basics-u3-l2/steps/1/options/1: A Bitcoin CFD at a broker
lessons/basics-u3-l2/steps/1/explanation: On an exchange you buy the coin itself. With a CFD (contract for difference) you only trade Bitcoin's price and have no coin to withdraw.
lessons/basics-u3-l2/steps/2/body: A **demo account** uses **virtual money** but **real market prices**. It's the perfect place to learn a platform and practice a strategy with zero risk. The catch? You don't feel the **fear and greed of real money**.
lessons/basics-u3-l2/steps/2/tip: Take your demo seriously: trade the same size and risk you plan to use with real money later.
lessons/basics-u3-l2/steps/3/statement: Good results on a demo account mean you'll get exactly the same results with real money.
lessons/basics-u3-l2/steps/3/explanation: With a real account, emotions come into play, and order fills can differ slightly too (like slippage). A demo is step one, not a guarantee.
lessons/basics-u3-l2/steps/4/prompt: What's the biggest limitation of a demo account?
lessons/basics-u3-l2/steps/4/options/0: You don't feel the fear and greed of real money
lessons/basics-u3-l2/steps/4/options/1: Its prices are fake and unrelated to the market
lessons/basics-u3-l2/steps/4/options/2: You can't place orders with it
lessons/basics-u3-l2/steps/4/options/3: You can only use it for one day
lessons/basics-u3-l2/steps/4/explanation: Demo prices come from the real market, and every order type is there. What's missing is the mental pressure of losing real money.
lessons/basics-u3-l2/steps/5/body: Before you deposit money, make sure the broker holds a **valid license (is regulated)** and the exchange has a solid **track record and security**. A promise of **guaranteed profit** means run; no market offers guaranteed profit.
lessons/basics-u3-l2/steps/5/tip: Start with a small amount and test a withdrawal first.
lessons/basics-u3-l2/steps/6/pairs/0/mea: The middleman who executes forex trades
lessons/basics-u3-l2/steps/6/pairs/1/mea: A marketplace for buying and selling crypto
lessons/basics-u3-l2/steps/6/pairs/2/mea: Trading the price without owning the asset
lessons/basics-u3-l2/steps/6/pairs/3/mea: A practice account with virtual money
lessons/basics-u3-l2/steps/7/sentence: In a ___ account you practice with virtual money but ___ market prices.
lessons/basics-u3-l2/steps/7/explanation: A demo shows live market prices, but the money is virtual. That's why practicing on it carries no risk.
lessons/basics-u3-l2/steps/8/prompt: Put the sensible path to starting trading in order.
lessons/basics-u3-l2/steps/8/items/0: Learn the basics and risk management
lessons/basics-u3-l2/steps/8/items/2: Open a real account with a little money
lessons/basics-u3-l2/steps/8/items/3: Grow your capital slowly once results are steady
lessons/basics-u3-l2/steps/8/explanation: Knowledge first, then risk-free practice, then a little real money so you experience the emotions too. Only add capital once your results are consistent.
lessons/basics-u3-l3/steps/0/body: **Technical analysis** means reading the **price chart**: trend, support and resistance, patterns and indicators. The idea is that traders' collective behavior leaves footprints on the chart and **behavior patterns** repeat.
lessons/basics-u3-l3/steps/1/body: **Fundamental analysis** looks for the **reason** behind price moves: interest rates, inflation, jobs and central bank decisions. In crypto, it also covers things like token supply and network usage.
lessons/basics-u3-l3/steps/2/prompt: Which of these is technical analysis?
lessons/basics-u3-l3/steps/2/options/0: Drawing support and resistance on the chart
lessons/basics-u3-l3/steps/2/explanation: Technical analysis works with the chart and price data. Inflation, central bank statements and unemployment are economic data, which makes them fundamental.
lessons/basics-u3-l3/steps/3/pairs/0/mea: The cost of money, set by the central bank
lessons/basics-u3-l3/steps/3/pairs/1/mea: The most common measure of inflation
lessons/basics-u3-l3/steps/3/pairs/2/mea: A calculation tool based on price data
lessons/basics-u3-l3/steps/4/body: Lots of traders **combine** the two: fundamentals tell you **why** and which way, technicals tell you **when and where**. Even if you only trade technicals, check the **economic calendar** before a trade; one big news release can wipe out any pattern within minutes.
lessons/basics-u3-l3/steps/5/prompt: A major economic report came out and the market reacted sharply. Tap the news candle.
lessons/basics-u3-l3/steps/5/explanation: This candle is several times longer than the others, and its volume spiked too: the classic footprint of big news. Before and after it, the market is much calmer.
lessons/basics-u3-l3/steps/6/statement: Done right, technical analysis predicts future prices with complete certainty.
lessons/basics-u3-l3/steps/6/explanation: No analysis gives certainty. Technical and fundamental analysis only tilt the odds in your favor. That's why you always need a stop loss.
lessons/basics-u3-l3/steps/7/prompt: Price is back at support and has formed a hammer. The economic calendar shows no major news today. What's more likely?
lessons/basics-u3-l3/steps/7/explanation: This support has already turned the price around once, and the hammer shows buyers are stepping in again. No major news also lowers the risk of a surprise move. Still, it's only better odds; put your stop loss below support.
lessons/basics-u3-l3/steps/8/prompt: Your technical analysis gives a buy signal, but the US jobs report (NFP) comes out in 10 minutes. What's the more careful move?
lessons/basics-u3-l3/steps/8/options/0: Wait until after the news or enter smaller
lessons/basics-u3-l3/steps/8/options/1: Enter with double size before the news
lessons/basics-u3-l3/steps/8/options/2: Remove the stop so news spikes can't hit it
lessons/basics-u3-l3/steps/8/options/3: Ignore the news; technicals are enough
lessons/basics-u3-l3/steps/8/explanation: Around major news, volatility and spreads can suddenly jump and price can spike either way. Waiting or trading smaller keeps your risk under control.
